lines: One key's own only entry is already old; another key has several recent updates.
Time-based retention runs over the whole log. Does it genuinely delete the old entry, even though it is that key's own latest?
answer: Retention never looks at a key at all.

lines: Run it for real: retention genuinely deleted the old entry, even though it was that key's own only, latest value.
Now run compaction over the identical log instead.
Does the old entry survive this time, just because it is still that key's own latest value?
answer: Compaction never checks age at all.

lines: Run it for real: compaction genuinely kept the old entry, because it is still that key's own latest value, with no age check at all.
steps.takeaway: Compaction has no age check at all; it only ever asks whether a value is still a key's own latest.

lines: A real tombstone, a message with the same key and no value, is appended after all the others.
Compaction runs past it. Does the key genuinely disappear entirely?
answer: The tombstone removes the key itself.

lines: Run it for real: the tombstone genuinely removed the key entirely, once compaction ran past it, with every other key genuinely untouched.
steps.takeaway: A tombstone removes the key itself from the log, not merely its most recent value.

lines: Two real, independent sources on this exact mechanism agree, in their own words.
Compaction keeps at least the last state for each key, and a null-payload message is treated as a real delete.
Run it for real, all together: time-based retention, keep-the-latest compaction, and the tombstone's own removal, all measured from the identical log.
steps.takeaway: Retention, compaction, and a tombstone are three genuinely different answers to how long data lasts.

lines: This whole chapter has been building toward one closed loop: how a log orders writes, how a consumer survives redelivery, and now, how long any of that even sticks around to be read.
A real tombstone's own removal is the last piece of that loop, closing the question this chapter opened.
So here's the real question underneath both of these mechanisms: how long should any one piece of data actually matter, and who gets to decide that, the clock or the key?
Retention never even looks at a key; it just watches a clock, which is exactly why it can erase something that still mattered, simply because enough time went by.

Compaction flips that completely: it watches keys, not clocks, so a value sticks around for as long as nothing newer has replaced it, and a tombstone is just the producer's own way of saying that this key's story is finally over.
